extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, dramatists, students of poetics, and literary critics
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evaluative criteria for composing tragic plays: definitions of tragedy and comedy, the six constituent parts of tragedy, rules for constructing plots, character-drawing, modes of discovery, and formal divisions of the play.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: A tragedy is the imitation of an action that is serious and also, as having magnitude, complete in itself; in language with pleasurable accessories, each kind brought in separately in the parts of the work; in a dramatic, not in a narrative form; with incidents arousing pity and fear, wherewith to accomplish its catharsis of such emotions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Key requirements: serious action; magnitude/wholeness; dramatic (not narrative) form; language enriched by rhythm/harmony/song; incidents must arouse pity and fear to achieve catharsis. Use examples (e.g. Oedipus) to test whether a work meets the definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Six Constituent Parts of Tragedy
rubrics_metrics.description: There are six parts consequently of every tragedy, viz. A Fable or Plot, Characters, Diction, Thought, Spectacle and Melody; two of them arising from the means, one from the manner, and three from the objects of the dramatic imitation; and there is nothing else besides these six.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat each as a distinct criterion: Plot (combination of incidents), Character (moral qualities revealed), Diction (composition of verses), Thought (what is said in proving points), Melody (song), Spectacle (stage appearance). Evaluate plays against each part and note that some elements (Melody, Diction, Thought) are ‘pleasurable accessories’ while Plot/Character are central to poetic art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Primacy of Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: The first essential, the life and soul, so to speak, of Tragedy is the Plot; and that the Characters come second. Tragedy is primarily an imitation of action, and it is mainly for the sake of the action that it imitates the personal agents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When judging or composing a tragedy, prioritize a well-constructed Plot (combination of incidents) over finely polished speeches or character detail. A play with strong plot but weaker diction often achieves tragi‑effect better than one with excellent diction but no coherent action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unity of Action (Unity of Plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: The story, as an imitation of action, must represent one action, a complete whole, with its several incidents so closely connected that the transposal or withdrawal of any one of them will disjoin and dislocate the whole.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unity is not 'one man as subject' but one coherent action (beginning, middle, end). Avoid episodic collections of unrelated events. Use the criterion: would removing any incident break the unity? If yes, it is a real part; if not, it is superfluous.

rubrics_metrics.name: Completeness and the Three Parts (Beginning, Middle, End)
rubrics_metrics.description: A whole is that which has beginning, middle, and end. A beginning is that which is not itself necessarily after anything else... and a middle, that which is by nature after one thing and has also another after it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Construct plots so that each section follows naturally: beginnings should lead to middles and middles to ends; beginnings / ends cannot be arbitrarily placed. Evaluate whether each stage is naturally connected to what follows/preceded it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Magnitude / Length of the Plot
rubrics_metrics.description: A story or Plot must be of some length, but of a length to be taken in by the memory... As a rough general formula, 'a length which allows of the hero passing by a series of probable or necessary stages from misfortune to happiness, or from happiness to misfortune', may suffice as a limit for the magnitude of the story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the plot is neither too minute (instantaneous) nor so vast that the unity is lost. Aim for a scope comprehensible in memory/performance and sufficient to show causal progression in the hero’s fortunes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid Episodic Plot (Anti-pattern)
rubrics_metrics.description: I call a Plot episodic when there is neither probability nor necessity in the sequence of episodes. Actions of this sort bad poets construct through their own fault, and good ones on account of the players.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid stitching together unrelated episodes merely to lengthen the piece. Ensure each episode follows by probability or necessity from what precedes and contributes to the whole action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peripety (Reversal)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Peripety is the change from one state of things within the play to its opposite of the kind described... the opposite state of things is produced by [incidents that follow with probability or necessity].
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peripety as a structural device to shift the hero’s fortunes plausibly; it should emerge from the plot’s causal chain (e.g. the Messenger’s arrival in Oedipus). Prefer peripeties that are probable/consequent rather than arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discovery (Anagnorisis)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Discovery is... a change from ignorance to knowledge, and thus to either love or hate, in the personages marked for good or evil fortune.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discovery should ideally arise from the incidents themselves (most artistic), or at least from reasoning or memory; avoid contrived poet-inserted revelations or overuse of external signs. Best dramatic effect when discovery combines with peripety.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffering (Pathos) as a Plot Element
rubrics_metrics.description: A third part is Suffering; which we may define as an action of a destructive or painful nature, such as murders on the stage, tortures, woundings, and the like.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suffering can be an essential element for tragic effect but should arise from the plot’s necessities, not gratuitously. Use suffering to heighten pity and fear when it follows plausibly from the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of Plot to Avoid
rubrics_metrics.description: There are three forms of Plot to be avoided. (1) A good man must not be seen passing from happiness to misery, or (2) a bad man from misery to happiness. ... (3) an extremely bad man be seen falling from happiness into misery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid plots that produce neither pity nor fear: (1) undeserved suffering on a fully good man is odious rather than piteous; (2) a bad man’s rise is untragic; (3) an extremely bad man’s fall produces no pity. Prefer the intermediate-type hero whose misfortune is partly undeserved.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ideal Tragic Hero (Type of Person to Depict)
rubrics_metrics.description: The intermediate kind of personage, a man not pre-eminently virtuous and just, whose misfortune, however, is brought upon him not by vice and depravity but by some error of judgement... the perfect Plot must have a single... the change in the hero's fortunes must be... from happiness to misery; and the cause of it must lie not in any depravity, but in some great error on his part.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose protagonists who are neither wholly virtuous nor wicked; their downfall should spring from a tragic error (hamartia) so the audience feels pity and fear and can identify with the hero.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce Pity and Fear by Plot, Not Spectacle
rubrics_metrics.description: The tragic fear and pity may be aroused by the Spectacle; but they may also be aroused by the very structure and incidents of the play—which is the better way and shows the better poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seek to evoke pity and fear through causal incident and discovery rather than relying on monstrous stage effects. If the recital of events (without sight) produces horror/pity, the plot is more artistically successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Spectacle as Least Artistic Element
rubrics_metrics.description: The Spectacle, though an attraction, is the least artistic of all the parts, and has least to do with the art of poetry... the getting-up of the Spectacle is more a matter for the costumier than the poet.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat spectacle as auxiliary: useful for performance but not as a substitute for strong plot and character. Avoid using spectacle to mask weaknesses in plot construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diction and Thought Defined and Distinguished
rubrics_metrics.description: By 'Diction' I mean merely this, the composition of the verses; and by 'Melody', what is too completely understood to require explanation... Third comes the element of Thought, i.e. the power of saying whatever can be said, or what is appropriate to the occasion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diction = verbal expression/verse craft; Thought = the ideas, arguments, and appropriateness of what characters say (rhetoric/political speech). Both matter, but they are subordinate to Plot in tragic effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character Crafting: Four Aims
rubrics_metrics.description: In the Characters there are four points to aim at. First and foremost, that they shall be good. ... The second point is to make them appropriate. The third is to make them like the reality... The fourth is to make them consistent and the same throughout.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When drawing characters: (1) moral goodness where appropriate; (2) appropriateness to role/gender/status; (3) likeness to believable human types; (4) internal consistency (even consistent inconsistency if that is the trait). Evaluate characters by these four aspects and watch for failures in incongruity or inconsistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Denouement Must Arise from Plot (Avoid Deus Ex Machina)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Denouement also should arise out of the plot itself, and not depend on a stage-artifice... The artifice must be reserved for matters outside the play—for past events beyond human knowledge, or events yet to come, which require to be foretold or announced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure the resolution follows from earlier incidents and character actions. Reserve miraculous or external contrivances only for events that are logically outside the dramatic present; avoid resolved endings produced by improbable stage artifices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Formal Divisions of Tragedy (Quantity/Sections)
rubrics_metrics.description: From the point of view of its quantity, a tragedy has the following parts: Prologue, Episode, Exode, and a choral portion, distinguished into Parode and Stasimon; these two are common to all tragedies, whereas songs from the stage and Commoe are only found in some. The Prologue is all that precedes the Parode of the chorus; an Episode all that comes in between two whole choral songs; the Exode all that follows after the last choral song. In the choral portion the Parode is the whole first statement of the chorus; a Stasimon, a song of the chorus without anapaests or trochees; a Commas, a lamentation sung by chorus and actor in concert.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these divisions to structure scenes and chorus involvement appropriately. Ensure episodes, choral songs, prologue, and exode serve the plot’s development rather than interrupting it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Species of Tragedy and Combining Elements
rubrics_metrics.description: There are four distinct species of Tragedy... first, the complex Tragedy, which is all Peripety and Discovery; second, the Tragedy of suffering; third, the Tragedy of character; the fourth constituent is that of 'Spectacle'... The poet's aim, then, should be to combine every element of interest, if possible, or else the more important and the major part of them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize different emphases (complex, suffering-focused, character-driven, spectacle-driven). Strive to combine major elements when possible, but be mindful of critics’ expectations and the poet’s particular strengths.

rubrics_metrics.name: Kinds of Discovery (ranked by artistry)
rubrics_metrics.description: Species of Discovery: (1) Discovery by signs or marks (least artistic); (2) Discoveries made directly by the poet (inartistic); (3) Discovery through memory; (4) Discovery through reasoning; (5) composite Discovery from bad reasoning; (6) Discovery arising from the incidents themselves (best).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer discoveries that emerge organically from the plot’s incidents. Avoid overly contrived sign-based or poet-inserted revelations. Use memory and reasoning when plausible, and aim for incident-driven recognition where possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical Composition Methods
rubrics_metrics.description: At the time when he is constructing his Plots, ... (1) to put the actual scenes as far as possible before his eyes; (2) the poet should even act his story with the very gestures of his personages; (3) his story... he should first simplify and reduce to a universal form, before proceeding to lengthen it out by the insertion of episodes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical advice for writers: visualize/observe scenes vividly; rehearse or mime actions to discover incongruities; reduce a story to its universal plot (what might happen) before adding episodes. Ensure episodes are appropriate and serve the central action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Complication and Denouement Distinction
rubrics_metrics.description: Every tragedy is in part Complication and in part Denouement; ... By Complication I mean all from the beginning of the story to the point just before the change in the hero's fortunes; by Denouement, all from the beginning of the change to the end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When constructing or evaluating a play, distinguish the material that establishes the situation (complication) from that which effects the reversal/resolution (denouement). Mastery of both phases is necessary; many dramatists succeed at complication but fail at denouement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do Not Dramatize an Entire Epic Body of Incident
rubrics_metrics.description: One should also remember... and not write a tragedy on an epic body of incident (i.e. one with a plurality of stories in it), by attempting to dramatize, for instance, the entire story of the Iliad.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid trying to compress large, multi-threaded epics into a single play; pick a portion with unity and work it as drama. Epic scale is unsuited to the tight unity required of tragedy.
